skip_reason: Existing-customer service-recovery call, not a sales conversation. Daniel is the North Austin branch manager calling a customer whose move has already been completed, to resolve a post-move billing dispute (a break charged to the customer and an overage against the quoted hours), issue a partial refund of $777 to the card on file, send a damage claim form for a broken mirror, and answer a question about a mover substitution. No quote is built, no estimate is given, no booking is attempted, and no pricing is presented to a prospect. The 85-point Sales Call Scorecard does not apply.
top_strength: Not scored — service-recovery call. Worth flagging as a model for how these should be handled, though. Daniel opened by owning the delay without being asked ('We do wanna apologize for the communication with yesterday. That was one of our training days that were shut down for'), which let the customer immediately de-escalate himself: 'sorry, I was just anxious to get a response. I could have been a little bit nicer.' He then did the thing most reps do not do on a dispute call, which is audit our own side against the evidence before the customer has to argue for it. On the break charge he went to the truck data rather than the paperwork: 'they put down as a zero minute break but they did stop on the between locations which yeah, GPS on the truck. So it's about a 26 minute break basically, just gonna do like a thirty minute back to you.' On the overage he volunteered that our own quote was wrong: 'I think it was under quoted a little bit... in my eyes I would have said probably more like a, like a six and a half to seven hour quote,' and he named the operational cause rather than blaming the crew — 'with the stairs, sometimes that is even pushing a three man job just to spread some that fatigue and then, yeah, you kind of getting the short of stick of having more fatigue kind of building up for just having the workload spread between two guys.' He also named the industry failure mode we position against and held us to it: 'in the moving industry, there's a, the tenancy of like a, like a bait and switch sort of thing. So, it's like, oh, this is gonna cost this much and then you know, day of, all of a sudden there's a bunch of extra fees... at the end of the day we don't want it to be where you feel that.' Net result on a customer who arrived angry: 'with this resolution and I mean, you've been great so I'll use you guys again too for the next move for sure.' That is a retained customer and a referral out of a billing dispute.
coaching_note: Not graded against the 85-point rubric — this is a claims and billing-resolution call, and it should be routed to the claims queue rather than the sales grading sample. Two things in it are worth pulling out for Amanda separately, though. First, and this is the important one: this call is hard evidence for the estimate-accuracy rock, and it is the cleanest example in this week's sample of what the 46% actually costs. The job was quoted at five and a half hours and ran ten. Daniel, reviewing it after the fact with the file in front of him, said the right number was 'more like a six and a half to seven hour quote,' and he identified exactly why the original was wrong — a two-bedroom with third-floor access and a long carry, quoted as if it were a flat two-bedroom. So this was not an unknowable move; it was a knowable move that was quoted without the access factored in. The bill for that single mis-quote was $777 refunded, roughly nine minutes of a branch manager's time, and a customer relationship that only survived because Daniel handled it well. That is the per-incident cost line that has been missing from the estimate-accuracy business case. Recommend this call get pulled as a case study for the bottom-4 review sessions — it is far more persuasive to a rep than a percentage, because the rep can hear the customer say 'I'm trying to budget and you know money's tight.' Second, the customer's complaint about the crew slowing down at the destination ('when they got to the new house James told me that it shouldn't take more than an hour and a half at most... they were bringing in like one item at a time') is a coaching signal for the crew and for whoever set that expectation on site. Daniel's own read was that an hour and a half to unload a two-bedroom is 'pretty optimistic' and that the real number is about two and a half — which means a crew lead verbally gave the customer a number that was roughly 40% below what the branch manager considers realistic, mid-move, on a job that was already running long. Verbal on-site re-quotes by crew leads are a second, separate estimate-accuracy leak worth checking for. Third, minor: Daniel told the customer the refund generates no notification — 'I don't think it notifies you at all. Yeah. It's usually a couple of business days and then it should just hit your account' — and the customer had to ask whether he could call back to check. A silent $777 refund on a customer who just went through a billing dispute is an avoidable second anxiety; a one-line confirmation email would close it.
phone_presence_notes: Led with an unprompted apology that defused the customer before any money was discussed, conceded fault on both our quote and our break-logging without hedging, checked the resolution rather than announcing it ('does that sound fair to you in terms of actual reimbursement there?'), and closed a billing dispute with the customer volunteering 'you've been great so I'll use you guys again too for the next move for sure.'
